<!--
THE BODY FIGURE, PROMOTED 2026-07-31 from Figure 3--figure supplement 1, which this file was until
that day. It carries ALL SEVEN members of the lattice, in cost-ladder order: LSE, NR, INR, R, MR,
VR, IR.

WHY SEVEN AND NOT FOUR (Luciano, 2026-07-31). The body used to walk four and this file widened it,
and holding two figures apart for the sake of two columns stopped making sense once every column
was carrying a claim the paper already makes in prose. Read as a factorial on the two switches,
interval averaging x recursion, the seven are not a ladder but a design in which each member answers
one question:
  NR   neither ingredient          r^2 1.153  X    accumulated 13.6  X
  INR  interval averaging alone    r^2 0.9995 v    accumulated 20.8  X
  R    recursion alone             r^2 0.782  X    accumulated  1.07 v
  IR   both                        r^2 0.999  v    accumulated  1.08 v
A double dissociation: the interval average repairs the data level and does nothing for the
accumulation, the recursion repairs the accumulation and does nothing for the data level, and only
the two together repair both. LSE sits outside the lattice, as the classical baseline.

MR AND VR ARE THE OTHER HALF OF THE ARGUMENT and are not decoration (Luciano, 2026-07-31). They say
that conditioning on ONE interval end is not enough, which is not obvious: MR is WORSE than R on the
ellipse-area measure, 1.63 against 1.17, so the intermediate rung does not interpolate between the
two ends of the step it sits in; and VR, which removes the between-endpoint variance without
restoring it in the gain, is worse still. The whole distance from R to IR is therefore in the update
and not in the variance (Discussion sec. 25).

READ EACH PANEL AGAINST THE GREEN LINE, NOT AGAINST ANOTHER COLUMN (Luciano, 2026-07-31). An earlier
version drew each class-B member over the member it is one step from, in grey. It was dropped: the
three comparisons it carried turned out to be small differences between two curves that both fail,
and a number in the caption states those better than a pale overlay does. What each panel claims is
that the member is or is not calibrated, and the calibrated value is drawn. The claim the figure
makes as a whole is that the family fails and IR is the exception, which is why IR is a column.

TWO-BLOCK Y SCALE ON ROWS B, D, F AND G, exactly the rows figure_3 splits, and for the same reason:
the open-loop members fail by a factor of twenty and the recursive ones by twenty percent, so one
axis cannot show both. On a shared scale the four recursive columns of the accumulated row collapse
onto the reference line and the MR-and-VR-against-IR difference, the number this figure exists for,
disappears. Rows A, C and E stay shared, where the magnitudes are comparable and a split would only
cost width. The supplements inherit this choice of which rows split rather than making their own, so they can
be read row for row against this figure.

THREE BLOCKS, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS THE TRAP (2026-08-03). The rows are not seven checks in a list,
they are the trace, then everything that can be checked WITHIN a sample, then everything that can
only be checked ACROSS samples. INR passes the whole middle block and fails the whole bottom one,
which is the dissociation this figure exists for, and a reader who reads row by row can miss it. The
strips are now filled by block and the E | F gap is opened, because E and F are the SAME quantity,
the information ratio, once per interval and once accumulated: the jump from 1.0 to 20.8 happens
between two adjacent rows whose titles differ by one word.
  A        the trace
  B C D E  per sample     -- INR passes every one
  F G      across time    -- INR fails both, by a factor of twenty

ROWS: the cascade, from the filter output through the residual to the accumulated score.
  A predicted & observed current   (one example recording, the same one in every column; the
    annotation is the ensemble-mean total logL, and read across the row it is the whole cost ladder)
  B residual variance  mean_t[r_t^2] ~ 1
  C per-step Fisher information  F_t   (no null: this row says WHERE each parameter is measured, and
    the shape being the same in all six columns is the claim that it belongs to the measurement)
  D score bias, standardized  sbar_t/sqrt(Fbar_t) ~ 0
  E per-interval information ratio  Var(s_t)/F_t ~ 1
  F accumulated information ratio  Var(sum s_t)/sum F_t ~ 1
  G autocorrelation (lag) ~ 0, THREE series (Luciano, 2026-07-31): the
    score for each parameter in its colour, and the parameter-free standardized RESIDUAL in neutral.
Rows A and B are parameter-free and drawn neutral; C to G carry k_off and N_ch, one colour each.
N_ch earns its place on row C, where it is the parameter whose information dies when the agonist is
washed out while k_off's does not, and on rows E and F, where VR fails harder on N_ch than on k_off.

INR REPLACED NMR 2026-07-31, and it is a different algorithm and not a relabel. `NMR` on disk is the
DEFECTIVE build that lost the N*ms interval-variance term to a refactor in a3e0a89, restored in
1f7138b; `macro_INR` is the method as published. Luciano ran it for this figure, so the column is
now the method rather than the broken build. The old dump is kept and its digest still builds, so
the two can be compared, but nothing in the paper draws it.

WHAT THE FIX BUYS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT, measured on the new run and the reason this column earns
its place. Restoring the interval variance repairs the DATA level completely: the mean squared
standardized residual is 0.9995 for INR against 1.3491 for the defective build and 1.1526 for NR,
and 0.9989 for IR, so on row B the non-recursive interval member is as well calibrated as the
boundary-conditioned filter. It repairs nothing at the INFERENCE level: the accumulated information
ratio is 20.8, worse than NR's 13.6, and the lag-one score autocorrelation is 0.868 against NR's
0.864. The likelihood is also 14.8 nats better than NR's.
That dissociation is the point. Diagnostics states that the residual check and the information check
fail independently, and that a member can pass the first and violate the second by an order of
magnitude. INR is that member: it passes the data-level check as well as IR does and misreports its
information by a factor of twenty. Nothing else in the paper demonstrates the claim; every other
member fails both checks together or passes both.

WIDTH, MEASURED ON Figure_3.pdf RATHER THAN ESTIMATED. The four body panels are 1.312 in each and
the fixed furniture eats 1.75 of the 7.0 in: 0.81 the left axis block, 0.30 the gap carrying the
second block's y axis, 0.08 per inter-column gap, 0.47 the rotated row-title strip. That furniture
does not scale with the column count, so six columns with all of it would leave 0.85 in per panel
and SEVEN leave about 0.72. Past four columns the row-title strip therefore goes to the caption and
the letters alone stay (see STRIP at the layout chunk), which buys back the 0.47 and lands the
panels near 0.79 in at seven columns. Measure the rendered PDF rather than trusting this arithmetic;
it is where the last two adjustments came from.

TWO SWITCHES, both at the read chunk, both named in the output file so variants coexist:
  PSEL    which parameters the score rows carry

DATA: the digests written by figure_3_digest.R, not the dumps. Seven members at ~9 to 16 MB each
instead of seven dumps at ~1 GB, so this renders on a laptop in about a minute. Cell: N_ch = 100,

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(patchwork)
```

```{r read}
# THE SWITCH. One entry per parameter to draw on the score rows. param_index in the digest:
# 0 = k_on, 1 = k_off, 2 = unitary_current, 5 = Num_ch_mean.
PSEL <- c(k_off = 1L, N_ch = 5L)          # set to c(k_off = 1L) for the one-parameter variant

# ROSTER. "steps" is the three class-B members drawn over the member each is one step from;
# "family" is the whole lattice with NO reference, every panel read against its own null.
# The second is the one the green-line reading argues for (Luciano, 2026-07-31): if a panel is read
# against the calibrated value and not against another algorithm, then the reference curve is
# cognitive load that buys three small differences between two failing curves, and those are better
# said as numbers in the caption. It also puts IR back in the frame, which the claim needs: the
# statement is that the whole family fails AND IR is the exception, and the exception has to be
# visible next to the failures.
ROSTER <- "family"
LAB  <- c(LSE = "LSE", ILSE = "ILSE", NR = "NR", INR = "INR", R = "R", MR = "MR", VR = "VR", IR = "IR")
FLAB <- c(LSE = "Least\nSquares", ILSE = "Interval Least\nSquares",
          NR = "Non-\nRecursive", INR = "Interval Non-\nRecursive",
          R = "Recursive", MR = "Mean\nRecursive", VR = "Variance\nRecursive",
          IR = "Interval\nRecursive")
# DIGEST TOKEN PER KEY, and the two least-squares entries are deliberately crossed. The dump written
# as ..._LSE is averaging_approximation = 1, so on the instantaneous/interval axis it is ILSE; the
# un-averaged arm added to figure_3_time.macroir on 2026-08-05 writes ..._LSE_av0 and is LSE. The
# files keep their names so nothing already reading them is silently relabelled, and the crossing is
# resolved here and only here, exactly as figure_1.Rmd does it.
DTOK <- c(LSE = "LSE_av0", ILSE = "LSE", NR = "NR", INR = "INR", R = "R", MR = "MR", VR = "VR", IR = "IR")
# `ref` is NA_character_ and not the logical NA, so that vapply over the roster stays type-stable
# whether or not the roster has references.
mk <- function(k, ref = NA_character_) list(key = k, ref = ref, lab = LAB[[k]], flab = FLAB[[k]],
                                 rlab = if (is.na(ref)) NA_character_ else LAB[[ref]])
STEPS <- if (ROSTER == "steps") {
  list(mk("INR", "NR"), mk("MR", "R"), mk("VR", "MR"))
} else {
  # ILSE inserted next to LSE, 2026-08-05, so the two least-squares arms read as the pair they are.
  # Everything after them keeps the cost-ladder order the header describes.
  lapply(c("LSE", "ILSE", "NR", "INR", "R", "MR", "VR", "IR"), mk)
}
HASREF <- !is.na(STEPS[[1]]$ref)
DEFAULT <- ROSTER == "family" && length(PSEL) == 2
OUT <- if (DEFAULT) "Figure_3.pdf" else
  sprintf("Figure_3_%s_%s.pdf", ROSTER, if (length(PSEL) == 1) "koff" else "both")

COLS <- vapply(STEPS, `[[`, "", "lab")
LEAD <- COLS[1]
B    <- 400    # bootstrap replicates over recordings

# Every member that appears anywhere, member or reference, read once.
NEED <- unique(na.omit(c(vapply(STEPS, `[[`, "", "key"), vapply(STEPS, function(s) s$ref, ""))))
dg <- setNames(lapply(NEED, function(a) {
  f <- sprintf("../data/digest/figure_3_digest_%s.rds", DTOK[[a]])
  if (!file.exists(f)) stop("missing digest for ", a, " (dump token ", DTOK[[a]],
                            "): run figure_3_digest.R ", DTOK[[a]])
  readRDS(f)
}), NEED)

SCAL <- rbindlist(lapply(NEED, function(a) as.data.table(dg[[a]]$scalar)[, key := a]))
PAR  <- rbindlist(lapply(NEED, function(a)
  as.data.table(dg[[a]]$param)[param_index %in% PSEL, .(simulation_index, sample_index,
                                                        param_index, s, I)][, key := a]))
PAR[, param := factor(names(PSEL)[match(param_index, PSEL)], levels = names(PSEL))]

# N_ch IS NOT DRAWN IN THE LEAST-SQUARES COLUMN, ported from the four-column parent this file
# replaced (figure_3.Rmd:145 there) and applied by figure_4_common.R through EXCLUDE_ROWS. Its
# diagonal information there is not zero, but it comes from the mean current N*i*P_open, along
# which the channel count and the unitary current are degenerate; separating them needs the gating
# fluctuations, the one thing least squares does not model. Measured rather than assumed: F_t over
# the pulse is 1076.55 for N_ch and for i alike, to every digit. The curve would therefore read as
# information about N_ch that least squares does not deliver. One filter here covers every row that
# descends from PAR, which is C to G. The legend has to say so, or the missing curve reads as a
# rendering failure (Luciano, 2026-07-30).
PAR_ALL <- copy(PAR)                       # kept whole: the degeneracy check needs the dropped curve
# Neither least-squares arm separates the channel number from the unitary current: the mean current
# depends on them only through their product, and it is the gating variance, absent from both, that
# breaks the tie. The exclusion therefore covers ILSE as well as LSE (widened 2026-08-05).
PAR <- PAR[!(param == "N_ch" & key %in% c("LSE", "ILSE"))]
tmap   <- unique(SCAL[key == NEED[1], .(sample_index, t, agonist)])[order(sample_index)]
n_samp <- nrow(tmap)
setorder(SCAL, key, simulation_index, sample_index)
setorder(PAR,  key, param, simulation_index, sample_index)
```

```{r stats}
set.seed(20260731)
colVar    <- function(M) { n <- nrow(M); m <- colMeans(M); (colMeans(M * M) - m^2) * n / (n - 1) }
rowCumsum <- function(M) t(apply(M, 1, cumsum))
wide <- function(d, val) as.matrix(dcast(d, simulation_index ~ sample_index, value.var = val)[, -1])

# Row B: residual variance over time, bootstrapped over recordings, like every other band here.
bootmean <- function(d, val) {
  M <- wide(d, val); n <- nrow(M)
  rep <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) colMeans(M[sample.int(n, n, TRUE), , drop = FALSE]),
                numeric(ncol(M)))
  data.table(sample_index = as.integer(colnames(M)), m = colMeans(M),
             lo = apply(rep, 1, quantile, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
             hi = apply(rep, 1, quantile, .975, na.rm = TRUE))
}
SCAL[, r2 := r_std^2]
RESID <- merge(SCAL[is.finite(r_std), bootmean(.SD, "r2"), by = key], tmap, by = "sample_index")

# Rows C to F out of ONE resampling loop per (member, parameter): the Fisher magnitude, the
# standardized score bias, the per-interval ratio and the accumulated ratio. The bias is resampled
# as the WHOLE ratio, colMeans(S)/sqrt(colMeans(I)), so it carries the correlation between the
# score and its own information rather than treating Fbar as known.
score_stats <- function(d) {
  Sm <- wide(d, "s"); Im <- wide(d, "I")
  smp <- as.integer(colnames(Sm)); n <- nrow(Sm)
  Fb <- colMeans(Im)
  repZ <- repF <- repB <- repC <- matrix(NA_real_, B, length(smp))
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    idx <- sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE)
    Sb <- Sm[idx, , drop = FALSE]; Ib <- Im[idx, , drop = FALSE]
    fb <- colMeans(Ib)
    repZ[b, ] <- colMeans(Sb) / sqrt(fb)
    repF[b, ] <- fb
    repB[b, ] <- colVar(Sb) / fb
    repC[b, ] <- colVar(rowCumsum(Sb)) / cumsum(fb)
  }
  ci <- function(M, p) apply(M, 2, quantile, p, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.table(sample_index = smp, Fbar = Fb,
             zA = colMeans(Sm) / sqrt(Fb), zA_lo = ci(repZ, .025), zA_hi = ci(repZ, .975),
             F_lo = ci(repF, .025), F_hi = ci(repF, .975),
             rB = colVar(Sm) / Fb, rB_lo = ci(repB, .025), rB_hi = ci(repB, .975),
             rC = colVar(rowCumsum(Sm)) / cumsum(Fb),
             rC_lo = ci(repC, .025), rC_hi = ci(repC, .975))
}
SCO <- merge(PAR[, score_stats(.SD), by = .(key, param)], tmap, by = "sample_index")

# Row G: score autocorrelation over lag. The bootstrap resamples the matrix of per-recording
# autocorrelations, so no autocorrelation is ever recomputed inside the loop.
LAGMAX  <- min(25, n_samp - 2)
acf_one <- function(x) as.numeric(acf(x, lag.max = LAGMAX, plot = FALSE)$acf)
# Factored out because row G now carries TWO kinds of series, the score per parameter and the
# parameter-free residual, and they have to be the same kind of object: one autocorrelation per
# recording, then a row-resample bootstrap of the stacked matrix. One estimator, called twice.
acf_boot <- function(d, val) {
  M <- do.call(rbind, d[, .(a = list(acf_one(get(val)))), by = simulation_index]$a)
  n <- nrow(M)
  rep <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) colMeans(M[sample.int(n, n, TRUE), , drop = FALSE]),
                numeric(ncol(M)))
  # list() and not .(): the data.table shorthand is only defined inside a `[` expression, and this
  # is a plain function called from two of them.
  list(lag = 0:LAGMAX, acf = colMeans(M),
       lo = apply(rep, 1, quantile, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
       hi = apply(rep, 1, quantile, .975, na.rm = TRUE))
}
# Mirrors the parent's row G, which took the residual in on 2026-07-31: the score is the memory that
# makes the accumulated ratio diverge, and the residual is the same memory at the data level and the
# only quantity here an experimentalist can compute on a real recording. Inheriting the parent's row
# content, as with its scale splits, is what lets the two figures be read row for row.
ACF <- rbind(
  PAR[, acf_boot(.SD, "s"), by = .(key, param)],
  SCAL[is.finite(r_std), acf_boot(.SD, "r_std"), by = key][, param := "residual"],
  use.names = TRUE)[lag >= 1]
ACF[, param := factor(as.character(param), levels = c("residual", names(PSEL)))]

# Row A: the ensemble-mean total logL over recordings and its SE. For this figure it is the number
# that carries the cost-ladder reading across the row, so it is computed for every member.
TOTL <- SCAL[, .(tot = sum(ll)), by = .(key, simulation_index)][
             , .(mean = mean(tot), se = sd(tot) / sqrt(.N)), by = key]
ES <- SCAL[, min(simulation_index)]
EX <- SCAL[simulation_index == ES, .(key, sample_index, t, agonist, obs = patch_current,
                                     y_mean, y_var)]

# ONE mask for the score rows, an absolute floor and not a fraction of the peak. What forces a mask
# is numerical (once the derivatives reach ~1e-15 the ratio is floating-point noise); a
# percent-of-peak threshold would erase the low-information region by construction, and with N_ch
# on the figure that region is exactly what row C is about.
FMIN <- 1e-6
dC <- SCO[is.finite(Fbar) & Fbar > FMIN]
dD <- SCO[is.finite(zA) & is.finite(Fbar) & Fbar > FMIN]
dE <- SCO[is.finite(rB) & is.finite(rB_lo) & rB_lo > 0 & is.finite(Fbar) & Fbar > FMIN]
dFa <- SCO[is.finite(rC) & is.finite(rC_lo) & rC_lo > 0]
```

```{r caption-numbers}
# --- the numbers the caption quotes, printed so they are never read off the plot (LINT-SRC) ---
PQ <- names(PSEL)[1]     # the parameter the quoted numbers are about
endv <- function(k, p) dFa[key == k & param == p][which.max(sample_index)]
cat("\n=== Figure 3 caption numbers (n_simulations =",
    uniqueN(SCAL$simulation_index), "| roster =", ROSTER,
    "| parameters drawn:", paste(names(PSEL), collapse = ", "), ") ===\n")

# WHAT EACH PANEL CLAIMS, AS A TEST AND NOT AS A PICTURE. With the roster read against the null and
# not against another member, the caption's job is to say which tests each member fails and by how
# much, so the table is one row per (member, parameter) with the two end-of-recording statistics
# and, for the time-resolved rows, the fraction of informative steps whose interval excludes the
# calibrated value. A 95% interval covers the null about 95% of the time when the member IS
# calibrated, so a fraction near 0.05 is a pass and anything far above it is not.
frac <- function(D, lo, hi, null) D[, .(f = mean(get(lo) > null | get(hi) < null)), by = .(key, param)]
tab <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = c("key", "param")), list(
  frac(dD, "zA_lo", "zA_hi", 0)[, .(key, param, D_bias = f)],
  frac(dE, "rB_lo", "rB_hi", 1)[, .(key, param, E_perint = f)],
  dFa[, .SD[which.max(sample_index)], by = .(key, param)][
      , .(key, param, F_accum = rC, F_lo = rC_lo, F_hi = rC_hi)],
  ACF[lag == 1, .(key, param, G_acf1 = acf, G_lo = lo, G_hi = hi)]))
tab <- merge(tab, TOTL[, .(key, logL = mean, logL_se = se)], by = "key")
tab[, `:=`(F_fails = F_lo > 1 | F_hi < 1, G_fails = G_lo > 0 | G_hi < 0)]
tab <- tab[order(match(key, vapply(STEPS, `[[`, "", "key")), param)]   # roster order, not alphabetical
print(as.data.frame(tab), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
# Row B is parameter-free, so it gets its own line.
cat("\nB residual variance, fraction of steps whose interval excludes 1:\n")
print(as.data.frame(RESID[, .(f = mean(lo > 1 | hi < 1)), by = key]), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

# THE SUM OF THE SCORE, AND THE FACTORISATION OF THE ACCUMULATED RATIO. Added 2026-08-12. Two
# quantities the figure implies and did not print:
#
#  (1) the accumulated score bias. Row D is PER INTERVAL, and what determines the estimator is the
#      sum, in which per-interval displacements of opposite sign can cancel. TWO THINGS HAVE TO BE
#      DONE IN ORDER AND THE SECOND IS NOT A DIVISION BY sqrt(F_aa): the first-order bias is the
#      VECTOR equation b = F^-1 g with g = E[sum_t s] and F the WHOLE information matrix, and the
#      displacement of one parameter in units of its marginal standard error is
#      b_a / sqrt((F^-1)_aa). Dividing the accumulated score of a parameter by the square root of
#      its own diagonal instead treats every other parameter as known, and at this cell that is not
#      a small difference: on N_ch it changes -0.34 into +0.82 for R, sign included, because the
#      channel number and the unitary current are strongly correlated. The diagonal reading is kept
#      in the printout as z_diag only to show how far off it is. F is rebuilt per recording from
#      the digest's dm, dv and y_var, F = sum_t (dm dm'/v + 0.5 dv dv'/v^2), which is the same
#      Gaussian-Fisher family used everywhere else in the paper; the bias in log10 units is printed
#      too, since that is what Figure 4 measures on fitted estimates and this predicts.
#
#  (2) the accumulated ratio. This one IS a per-direction statement and needs no inverse: it is a
#      ratio of two scalars in one direction, and exactly, at every T,
#          Var(sum s_t)/sum F_t  =  [sum Var(s_t)/sum F_t] * [Var(sum s_t)/sum Var(s_t)],
#      the first factor being row E weighted by the information and the second the correlation that
#      row G is about. Printed together because the reading is WHICH of the two a member fails, and
#      the answer is not the one the accumulated ratio alone suggests.
#
# Own seed, so this block neither moves nor is moved by the stats chunk's draws.
set.seed(20260812)

# (2) the factorisation, per drawn parameter, on the objects the rest of the chunk already uses.
accum_one <- function(d) {
  Sm <- wide(d, "s"); Im <- wide(d, "I")
  Fb <- colMeans(Im); n <- nrow(Sm)
  i  <- seq_len(max(which(is.finite(Fb) & Fb > FMIN)))    # up to the last informative step, as dFa
  Ss <- rowSums(Sm[, i, drop = FALSE]); Fs <- sum(Fb[i])
  Vs <- sum(colVar(Sm[, i, drop = FALSE]))
  rep <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
    j  <- sample.int(n, n, TRUE)
    sb <- rowSums(Sm[j, i, drop = FALSE]); vb <- sum(colVar(Sm[j, i, drop = FALSE]))
    c(vb / sum(colMeans(Im[j, i, drop = FALSE])), var(sb) / vb)
  }, numeric(2))
  ci <- function(r, p) quantile(rep[r, ], p, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.table(Ebar = Vs / Fs,      Ebar_lo = ci(1, .025), Ebar_hi = ci(1, .975),
             infl = var(Ss) / Vs, infl_lo = ci(2, .025), infl_hi = ci(2, .975),
             accum = var(Ss) / Fs)
}
KEYS <- vapply(STEPS, `[[`, "", "key")
ACC <- PAR[, accum_one(.SD), by = .(key, param)][order(match(key, KEYS), param)]
ACC[, `:=`(E_fails = Ebar_lo > 1 | Ebar_hi < 1, i_fails = infl_lo > 1 | infl_hi < 1)]
cat("\nJ_T/F_T = Ebar * inflation, per drawn parameter:\n")
print(as.data.frame(ACC), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

# (1) the accumulated bias, over ALL FOUR identified parameters at once, since it needs the whole
# matrix. Read straight from the digests: PAR keeps only s and I, and this needs dm, dv and y_var.
PIDS <- c(k_on = 0L, k_off = 1L, i = 2L, N_ch = 5L)
bias_one <- function(a) {
  d <- as.data.table(dg[[a]]$param)[param_index %in% PIDS]
  if (a %in% c("LSE", "ILSE")) d <- d[param_index != 5L]   # degenerate with i, excluded
  d <- merge(d, as.data.table(dg[[a]]$scalar)[, .(simulation_index, sample_index, y_var)],
             by = c("simulation_index", "sample_index"))[is.finite(y_var) & y_var > 0]
  ids <- sort(unique(d$param_index)); np <- length(ids)
  W <- dcast(d, simulation_index + sample_index + y_var ~ param_index, value.var = c("s","dm","dv"))
  sims <- sort(unique(W$simulation_index)); n <- length(sims); g0 <- match(W$simulation_index, sims)
  DM <- as.matrix(W[, paste0("dm_", ids), with = FALSE])
  DV <- as.matrix(W[, paste0("dv_", ids), with = FALSE])
  gi <- rowsum(as.matrix(W[, paste0("s_", ids), with = FALSE]), g0)   # score summed per recording
  Fi <- array(0, c(n, np, np))                                        # information per recording
  for (p in seq_len(np)) for (q in seq_len(np))
    Fi[, p, q] <- rowsum(DM[, p] * DM[, q] / W$y_var +
                         0.5 * DV[, p] * DV[, q] / W$y_var^2, g0)
  stat <- function(j) {
    Fm <- apply(Fi[j, , , drop = FALSE], c(2, 3), mean); Fv <- solve(Fm)
    bv <- as.vector(Fv %*% colMeans(gi[j, , drop = FALSE]))
    list(z = bv / sqrt(diag(Fv)), b = bv,
         zd = colMeans(gi[j, , drop = FALSE]) / sqrt(diag(Fm)))
  }
  o <- stat(seq_len(n))
  rp <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) stat(sample.int(n, n, TRUE))$z, numeric(np))
  # `key` cannot be passed to data.table(), which reads it as its own argument, so it is set after.
  out <- data.table(param = names(PIDS)[match(ids, PIDS)], z = o$z,
                    lo = apply(rp, 1, quantile, .025), hi = apply(rp, 1, quantile, .975),
                    bias_log10 = o$b, z_diag = o$zd)
  out[, key := a]; setcolorder(out, c("key", "param"))[]
}
BIAS <- rbindlist(lapply(KEYS, bias_one))
BIAS[, covers0 := lo < 0 & hi > 0]
cat("\nAccumulated score bias, b = F^-1 E[sum s], in marginal standard errors (z);",
    "z_diag is the diagonal-only reading, kept to show the gap:\n")
print(as.data.frame(BIAS), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
if (HASREF) for (i in seq_along(STEPS)) cat(sprintf(
  "%-4s - %-3s: %+7.2f nats total logL | accumulated ratio %.3f vs %.3f\n",
  STEPS[[i]]$lab, STEPS[[i]]$rlab,
  TOTL[key == STEPS[[i]]$key, mean] - TOTL[key == STEPS[[i]]$ref, mean],
  endv(STEPS[[i]]$key, PQ)$rC, endv(STEPS[[i]]$ref, PQ)$rC))

# THE COLUMN THIS FIGURE GAINED, as numbers rather than as an eyeball. INR restores the interval
# variance term that the archived NMR build had lost, and what that buys is a DATA-level repair with
# no INFERENCE-level repair: row B goes to one while rows F and G stay broken. Printed against both
# neighbours, the member one step below it on the ladder (NR) and the calibrated member (IR), since
# the claim is that it matches the second on row B and the first on rows F and G.
if ("INR" %in% NEED) {
  b_of <- function(k) RESID[key == k, mean(m)]
  f_of <- function(k) endv(k, PQ)$rC
  g_of <- function(k) ACF[key == k & param == PQ & lag == 1, acf]
  cat("\nINR, the interval non-recursive member, against its neighbours:\n")
  for (k in intersect(c("NR", "INR", "IR"), NEED))
    cat(sprintf("  %-4s mean r^2 %.4f | accumulated J/F %6.2f | score ACF(1) %+.4f | logL %8.2f\n",
                LAB[[k]], b_of(k), f_of(k), g_of(k), TOTL[key == k, mean]))
  cat(sprintf("  INR - NR = %+.2f nats; INR reaches IR's residual calibration (%.4f vs %.4f)\n",
              TOTL[key == "INR", mean] - TOTL[key == "NR", mean], b_of("INR"), b_of("IR")))
  cat("  and does not reach its information calibration:",
      sprintf("%.2f against %.2f.\n", f_of("INR"), f_of("IR")))
}
```

```{r panels, fig.width = 7.0, fig.height = 7.5}
# MEMBER / REFERENCE. With one parameter the colour is free, so the member is the body figure's
# blue and the reference is grey: the strongest possible contrast for the comparison this figure
# exists to make. With two parameters the colour has to carry the PARAMETER, so the contrast moves
# to weight and opacity: the reference is the same hue, thicker and washed out, the member is thin,
# saturated and the only one with a band. Dashing was the other candidate and was rejected because
# rows D to F are high-frequency at 0.4 pt, where a dash pattern reads as noise.
PCOL <- c(residual = "#1A1A1A", k_off = "#0072B2", N_ch = "#D55E00")
PLEG <- c(residual = expression(r[t]), k_off = expression(k["off"]), N_ch = expression(N["ch"]))
# alpha 0.35 at linewidth 0.85 was tried first and failed: against a 0.4 pt member of the same hue
# the two curves read as two curves, with no cue as to which is which. The contrast has to be in
# WEIGHT, not only in opacity, so the reference becomes a pale wide underlay that the member rides
# on: nothing else in the figure is 1.3 pt, so the idiom is unambiguous at a glance.
REF_A <- if (length(PSEL) == 1) 1.00 else 0.30    # reference opacity
REF_W <- if (length(PSEL) == 1) 0.55 else 1.30    # reference weight
REF_C <- if (length(PSEL) == 1) "grey60" else NA  # reference colour, NA = take the parameter's
# Rows A and B are parameter-free, so their colour is free and the reference can be plain grey at a
# normal weight. Only the score rows need the pale-wide-underlay trick, because there the hue is
# spoken for by the parameter.
NEU_L <- "#1A1A1A"; NEU_F <- "#9E9E9E"; NEU_R <- "grey55"; NEU_W <- 0.55
NUL   <- "#009E73"

pscale <- list(scale_colour_manual(values = PCOL, labels = PLEG, name = NULL, drop = FALSE),
               scale_fill_manual(values = PCOL, labels = PLEG, name = NULL, drop = FALSE))
# The reference layer: same hue when the colour is spoken for, flat grey when it is not.
refdat  <- function(D, s) if (HASREF) D[key == s$ref] else D[0]
reflayer <- function(d, mapping) {
  if (!HASREF || !nrow(d)) return(NULL)
  if (is.na(REF_C)) {
    geom_line(data = d, mapping = mapping, linewidth = REF_W, alpha = REF_A, show.legend = FALSE)
  } else {
    geom_line(data = d, mapping = mapping, colour = REF_C, linewidth = REF_W, show.legend = FALSE)
  }
}

# Y SCALES, and which one is right follows from WHAT THE PANEL IS COMPARED TO.
#   with a reference: the comparison is between two curves INSIDE the panel, so the scale is PER
#     COLUMN. A shared scale hands the range to whichever step is largest -- the first spans 13 to
#     22 in the accumulated row while the other two span 1.07 to 1.20 -- and renders the
#     MR-against-R difference, a number the paper quotes, as a flat line.
#   without a reference: the comparison is between the curve and its null, and the null is the same
#     value in every column, so the scale is SHARED per row and the columns become comparable for
#     free. This also returns the width that a second y axis was costing.
rng <- function(D, s, cols, incl = NULL) {
  d <- if (HASREF) D[key %in% c(s$key, s$ref)] else D
  v <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) d[[k]]))
  range(c(v[is.finite(v)], incl), finite = TRUE)
}

# THE TWO-BLOCK SPLIT, and it is the parent figure's, not a new invention. The open-loop members
# fail by a factor of twenty and the recursive ones by twenty percent, so one axis cannot show
# both: on a shared scale the four recursive columns of the accumulated row collapse onto the
# reference line and the MR-and-VR-against-IR difference, which is the number this figure exists
# for, disappears. figure_3.Rmd splits exactly rows B, D, F and G and leaves A, C and E shared;
# this figure inherits that choice rather than making its own, so the two can be read row for row.
# ILSE added 2026-08-05. It is open-loop like the other three: no update, so its accumulated
# information ratio fails by the same order and it belongs on the same axis as LSE, NR and INR,
# not on the recursive one where anything omitted from this list silently lands. The block is
# now four and four. NMR is the pre-2026-08-01 name of INR and is kept so an old roster still
# splits correctly.
NAIVE <- intersect(COLS, c("LSE", "ILSE", "NR", "INR", "NMR"))
blkof <- function(lab) if (lab %in% NAIVE) "naive" else "rec"
KEYBLK <- setNames(vapply(STEPS, function(s) blkof(s$lab), ""), vapply(STEPS, `[[`, "", "key"))
# The first column of each block carries the y numbers; only the first of the figure carries the
# y title, since it is the same quantity on both scales.
AXIS_AT <- c(COLS[1], if (length(unique(KEYBLK)) > 1) COLS[which(vapply(COLS, blkof, "") == "rec")[1]])
# Per-block range. `pad` and the log/linear treatment stay with the caller, as in the flat case.
rng2 <- function(D, cols, incl = NULL) {
  lapply(split(names(KEYBLK), KEYBLK), function(ks) {
    v <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) D[key %in% ks][[k]]))
    range(c(v[is.finite(v)], incl), finite = TRUE)
  })
}
qrng2 <- function(D, cols, p = c(.005, .995)) {
  lapply(split(names(KEYBLK), KEYBLK), function(ks) {
    v <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) D[key %in% ks][[k]]))
    as.numeric(quantile(v[is.finite(v)], p))
  })
}
pick <- function(yl, s) if (is.list(yl)) yl[[blkof(s$lab)]] else yl

base <- function() theme_bw(base_size = 9)
tr   <- range(tmap$t)
lr   <- range(c(1, ACF$lag))
agon <- tmap[agonist > 0]; x0 <- min(agon$t); x1 <- max(agon$t)
# AGONIST BAND, -Inf/Inf and not +-1e10 (fixed 2026-07-31). A rect 2e10 tall clipped to a window of
# order one rasterises to NOTHING on a linear axis, so every LINEAR row of this figure was rendering
# unshaded while the log rows were fine -- inconsistent shading inside one figure, which reads as
# deliberate and was not. -Inf/Inf means "to the panel edge"; on a log axis it is NaN and the layer
# is dropped, hence the tiny positive lower bound there instead.
mkshade <- function(logr = FALSE) annotate("rect", xmin = x0, xmax = x1,
                  ymin = if (logr) 1e-300 else -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = .5)
padr <- function(r, f = .06) r + c(-1, 1) * diff(r) * f

ratio_breaks <- function(lo, hi) {
  cand <- if (log10(hi) - log10(lo) <= 1.2)
            c(.1, .2, .3, .5, .7, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100)
          else c(.1, .2, .5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
  b <- sort(unique(c(1, cand[cand >= lo & cand <= hi])))
  if (length(b) > 3) b <- sort(unique(c(b[1], 1, b[length(b)])))
  b
}
# Signed axes: at most three breaks, SYMMETRIC about zero. The body figure's rule (keep the first
# break, zero, and the last) can return -0.2 / 0 / 0.1, which reads as a mistake; here the outer
# pair is one round step chosen to fit inside the range.
sym_breaks <- function(ylim) {
  s <- max(abs(ylim)); st <- c(.005, .01, .02, .05, .1, .2, .5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)
  st <- st[st <= s]; if (!length(st)) return(0)
  k <- st[length(st)]; b <- c(-k, 0, k)
  sort(unique(b[b >= ylim[1] & b <= ylim[2]]))
}
deco <- function(p, col, xr, ylim, yq, bottom = FALSE, xlab = NULL, logr = FALSE, own = FALSE,
                 split = FALSE) {
  if (logr) {
    ylim <- c(min(ylim[1], 1), max(ylim[2], 1))
    rb <- ratio_breaks(ylim[1], ylim[2])
    p <- p + scale_y_log10(breaks = rb, labels = as.character(rb)) +
      coord_cartesian(xlim = xr, ylim = ylim)
  } else {
    p <- p + scale_y_continuous(breaks = sym_breaks(ylim)) + coord_cartesian(xlim = xr, ylim = ylim)
  }
  # Who prints y numbers. `own` (per-column scales) means everybody, because hiding them would
  # silently invite a comparison across columns whose scales differ. `split` means the first column
  # of each block. Otherwise the leftmost alone. The y TITLE appears once in every case, because it
  # is the same quantity whatever the scale.
  shows <- own || (split && col %in% AXIS_AT)
  if (col == LEAD) p <- p + ylab(yq) + theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8))
  else if (shows) p <- p + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())
  else p <- p + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
                      axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
  if (bottom) {
    if (col == COLS[2]) p <- p + xlab(xlab) + theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8))
    else p <- p + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank())
  } else p <- p + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
  p + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(0.5, 3, 0.5, 3))
}

# Column heads name the STEP, not the member.
colhead <- function(s) ggplot() + theme_void() +
  ggtitle(if (HASREF) bquote(bold(.(s$lab)) ~ "over" ~ .(s$rlab)) else bquote(bold(.(s$lab))),
          subtitle = s$flab) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = .5, size = 9, margin = margin(b = 0.5)),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = .5, size = 7, margin = margin(b = 0)),
        plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
rowlet <- function(lt) ggplot() + theme_void() +
  annotate("text", x = .5, y = .97, label = lt, size = 8 / .pt, fontface = "bold", vjust = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
rowstrip <- function(txt, fill = "grey85", ymin = .03, ymax = .97) ggplot() + theme_void() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = .15, xmax = 1, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = fill, colour = NA) +
  annotate("text", x = .575, y = .5, label = txt, angle = -90, size = 6.5 / .pt, lineheight = .9) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))

# THE ROWS ARE THREE BLOCKS AND THE FIGURE NOW SAYS SO, because the distinction between what is
# checked WITHIN a sample and what is checked ACROSS samples is the claim, not a detail of layout.
# A is the trace. B to E are per-sample checks, every one of which INR PASSES. F and G are the
# across-time checks, both of which INR fails, by a factor of twenty. A reader who does not see that
# the middle block passes as a block and the bottom block fails as a block has been shown the
# dissociation and has not been told it.
#
# The boundary that carries it is E | F, and it is the only one that has to be unmissable: E and F
# are the SAME quantity, the information ratio, once per interval and once accumulated, so the jump
# from 1.0 to 20.8 happens between two adjacent rows whose titles differ by one word. Marked by a
# change of HUE and not of lightness, and not by a gap. A gap was tried first and abandoned: it
# depends on which end of the strip cell y = 1 is, the first attempt put the break above E and below
# F (grouping the two boundaries that carry nothing), and the correction did not land either. Hue is
# orientation-free, costs no width (the strip column is a fixed 0.203 in, and in patchwork a fixed
# width in one row is reserved in EVERY row), keeps 6.5 pt black text legible, and is redundant with
# the row titles, so nothing rests on colour alone.
#
# NO REORDERING, and the earlier plan to move the Fisher row up was WRONG. F_t is a per-sample
# quantity, and it is the denominator of row E, so it belongs exactly where it is. The blocks are
# already contiguous; only the marking was missing.
RSTRIP_FILL <- c(A = "grey90", B = "grey85", C = "grey85", D = "grey85", E = "grey85",
                 F = "#BFCAD4", G = "#BFCAD4")
RSTRIP_YMIN <- c(A = .03, B = .03, C = .03, D = .03, E = .03, F = .03, G = .03)
RSTRIP_YMAX <- c(A = .97, B = .97, C = .97, D = .97, E = .97, F = .97, G = .97)

# "per-step" said twice more, so the middle block is named by its own titles and needs no fourth
# line of strip text (a third rotated line would widen the fixed column in every row). E and F
# already carry "per-interval" and "accumulated", which is the contrast the block boundary marks.
# E AND F SHORTENED 2026-08-12, and the reason is arithmetic rather than taste. The strip text is
# rotated, so its LENGTH is measured against the ROW HEIGHT. With HS giving E 0.60 of 4.85 units in
# a 5.728 in grid, E's row is 0.709 in = 51 pt, and "information ratio" at 6.5 pt is 17 characters,
# about 53 pt. It did not fit and spilled into the neighbouring rows, which is what showed as E and
# F running into each other. Dropping the word takes the longest line to 12 characters, about 37 pt
# in a 51 pt row. What the comment below requires is preserved: E and F still differ by ONE word,
# which is the whole point of that boundary, and the quantity itself is named by the y axis
# (Var(s_t)/F_t against Var(Sigma s_t)/Sigma F_t) and by the legend.
RTTL <- c(A = "predicted &\nobserved current", B = "residual\nvariance",
          C = "per-step\ninformation", D = "per-step\nscore bias",
          E = "per-interval\nratio",
          F = "accumulated\nratio", G = "autocorrelation")

# --- A: the example recording, the same one in every column. The member's predictive band and
# mean, the reference's mean as a line but NOT its band: two overlapping +-1 sd ribbons in a 1.78 in
# panel read as one wide ribbon. Both total logL values are annotated, which is where the ladder
# identity stops being a visual impression and becomes a number.
yTr <- padr(range(c(EX$obs, EX$y_mean - sqrt(EX$y_var), EX$y_mean + sqrt(EX$y_var)), na.rm = TRUE))
yTr[2] <- yTr[2] + 0.45 * diff(yTr)
pA <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- EX[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(EX, s)
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t)) + mkshade() +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = y_mean - sqrt(y_var), ymax = y_mean + sqrt(y_var)),
                fill = NEU_F, alpha = .5) +
    geom_point(aes(y = obs), colour = "grey45", size = .35, alpha = .5) +
    geom_line(data = r, aes(y = y_mean), colour = NEU_R, linewidth = .55) +
    geom_line(aes(y = y_mean), colour = NEU_L, linewidth = .4) +
    annotate("text", x = tr[2], y = yTr[2], hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 2.5, lineheight = .95,
             label = if (HASREF)
               sprintf("mean logL\n%s %.1f\n%s %.1f", s$lab, TOTL[key == s$key, mean],
                       s$rlab, TOTL[key == s$ref, mean])
             else sprintf("mean logL\n%.1f %s %.1f", TOTL[key == s$key, mean], "\u00b1",
                             TOTL[key == s$key, se])) + base()
  deco(g, s$lab, tr, yTr, "current")
})
# --- B: residual variance
RESID[, lo_p := pmax(lo, 1e-6)]
pB <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- RESID[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(RESID, s)
  yB <- lapply(rng2(RESID, c("lo_p", "hi"), incl = 1), function(r) 10^padr(log10(r)))
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t, m)) + mkshade(TRUE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = NUL, linewidth = .4) +
    geom_line(data = r, colour = NEU_R, linewidth = NEU_W) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo_p, ymax = hi), fill = NEU_F, alpha = .45) +
    geom_line(colour = NEU_L, linewidth = .4) + base()
  deco(g, s$lab, tr, pick(yB, s), expression(bar(r[t]^2)), logr = TRUE, own = HASREF, split = TRUE)
})
# --- C: log10 F_t on a LINEAR axis. The limits come from the CURVE, not from the band's lower edge:
# F_lo runs down to the mask floor, and ranging over the band there spends two thirds of the row on
# empty space (the defect the body figure's row C has and this one does not repeat).
dC[, `:=`(lF = log10(Fbar), lF_lo = log10(pmax(F_lo, 1e-300)), lF_hi = log10(F_hi))]
# The floor is the top of the range minus DEC decades, not the minimum of the curve. The N_ch
# information falls off a cliff when the agonist is washed out and keeps falling to the mask, so
# ranging over the curve spends most of the row drawing the cliff. Five decades keep the plateau,
# the cliff and where each parameter stops being measured, which is what the row is for; the tail
# below runs off the panel and the caption says so.
DEC <- 5
pC <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- dC[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(dC, s)
  hi <- rng(dC, s, c("lF_hi"))[2]
  yC <- padr(c(hi - DEC, hi), .04)
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t, lF, colour = param, fill = param)) + mkshade() +
    reflayer(r, aes(t, lF, colour = param)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lF_lo, ymax = lF_hi), alpha = .22, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .4, show.legend = FALSE) + base() + pscale +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = tr, ylim = yC) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty(yC, n = 3)) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(0.5, 3, 0.5, 3),
          axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
  if (s$lab == LEAD) g + ylab(expression(log[10] ~ F[t])) +
      theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8))
  else if (HASREF) g + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())
  else g + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
                 axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
})
# --- D: standardized score bias. Percentile limits and not extremes: one excursion at the
# concentration jump would otherwise set the scale for the whole row.
qrng <- function(D, s, cols, p = c(.005, .995)) {
  d <- if (HASREF) D[key %in% c(s$key, s$ref)] else D
  v <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) d[[k]]))
  as.numeric(quantile(v[is.finite(v)], p))
}
pD <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- dD[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(dD, s)
  yD <- lapply(qrng2(dD, c("zA_lo", "zA_hi")), padr, .08)
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t, zA, colour = param, fill = param)) + mkshade() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = NUL, linewidth = .4) +
    reflayer(r, aes(t, zA, colour = param)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = zA_lo, ymax = zA_hi), alpha = .22, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .4, show.legend = FALSE) + base() + pscale
  deco(g, s$lab, tr, pick(yD, s), expression(bar(s)[t] / sqrt(F[t])), own = HASREF, split = TRUE)
})
# --- E: per-interval information ratio
pE <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- dE[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(dE, s)
  yE <- 10^padr(log10(qrng(dE, s, c("rB_lo", "rB_hi"), c(.01, .99))))
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t, rB, colour = param, fill = param)) + mkshade(TRUE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = NUL, linewidth = .4) +
    reflayer(r, aes(t, rB, colour = param)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rB_lo, ymax = rB_hi), alpha = .22, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .4, show.legend = FALSE) + base() + pscale
  deco(g, s$lab, tr, yE, expression(Var(s[t]) / F[t]), logr = TRUE, own = HASREF)
})
# --- F: accumulated information ratio, bottom of the time block
pF <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- dFa[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(dFa, s)
  yF <- lapply(rng2(dFa, c("rC_lo", "rC_hi"), incl = 1), function(r) 10^padr(log10(r)))
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(t, rC, colour = param, fill = param)) + mkshade(TRUE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = NUL, linewidth = .4) +
    reflayer(r, aes(t, rC, colour = param)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rC_lo, ymax = rC_hi), alpha = .22, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .4, show.legend = FALSE) + base() + pscale
  # Sigma AS A SYMBOL, NOT AS sum(). Changed 2026-08-12: plotmath's sum() sets a DISPLAY-size
  # operator, so the summation signs came out taller than the rest of the label and, rotated into
  # the y axis, made this the widest label of the seven. `Sigma` is the same character at text size.
  deco(g, s$lab, tr, pick(yF, s), expression(Var(Sigma * s[t]) / Sigma * F[t]),
       bottom = TRUE, xlab = "time (ms)", logr = TRUE, own = HASREF, split = TRUE)
})
# --- G: score autocorrelation over lag, bottom of the lag block
pG <- lapply(STEPS, function(s) {
  d <- ACF[key == s$key]; r <- refdat(ACF, s)
  yG <- lapply(rng2(ACF, c("lo", "hi"), incl = 0), padr, .08)
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(lag, acf, colour = param)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = NUL, linewidth = .4) +
    reflayer(r, aes(lag, acf, colour = param)) +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = .35, show.legend = FALSE,
                   position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
    geom_point(size = .3, position = position_dodge(width = .4), show.legend = FALSE) +
    base() + pscale
  deco(g, s$lab, lr, pick(yG, s), "ACF", bottom = TRUE, xlab = "lag", own = HASREF, split = TRUE)
})

# ONE hand-drawn key, in the layout's last row. Hand-drawn rather than collected, because the
# member/reference distinction is weight and opacity applied inside geoms and has no scale for
# patchwork to collect, and because guides = "collect" only merges guides that are IDENTICAL.
# Positions are in panel fractions, so a label that is too long silently overprints its neighbour
# (it did, on the first render). They are laid out from a single vector of column starts, measured
# against the longest label at 6.5 pt rather than guessed.
keyplot <- local({
  seg <- function(x, y, col, lw, a = 1)
    annotate("segment", x = x, xend = x + .045, y = y, yend = y, colour = col, linewidth = lw,
             alpha = a)
  txt <- function(x, y, lab, parse = FALSE)
    annotate("text", x = x + .056, y = y, hjust = 0, size = 6.5 / .pt, label = lab, parse = parse)
  y1 <- if (HASREF && length(PSEL) > 1) .74 else .5
  g <- ggplot()
  if (HASREF) g <- g +
    seg(.015, y1, if (is.na(REF_C)) "grey35" else REF_C, REF_W, REF_A) +
    txt(.015, y1, "the member it is one step from") +
    seg(.44, y1, PCOL[[1]], .5) +
    txt(.44, y1, "the step's member, with its 95% bootstrap interval")
  if (length(PSEL) > 1) {
    y2 <- if (HASREF) .26 else .5
    # Three keys since row G took the residual in: the two score parameters, and the residual, whose
    # scope has to be named or a reader looks for a black curve on rows C to F and does not find one.
    # Kept SHORT. The first version carried the rows-A-and-B sentence here too and ran off the right
    # edge of the page, silently: the key is drawn in panel fractions, so an over-long label does not
    # wrap, it disappears. Anything longer than a clause belongs in the caption.
    g <- g + seg(.015, y2, PCOL[["k_off"]], .5) + txt(.015, y2, 'k["off"]', parse = TRUE) +
      seg(.105, y2, PCOL[["N_ch"]], .5) + txt(.105, y2, 'N["ch"]', parse = TRUE) +
      annotate("text", x = .195, y = y2, hjust = 0, size = 6.5 / .pt,
               label = "score, rows C to G") +
      seg(.375, y2, PCOL[["residual"]], .5) + txt(.375, y2, 'r[t]', parse = TRUE) +
      annotate("text", x = .445, y = y2, hjust = 0, size = 6.5 / .pt,
               label = "standardized residual, row G")
  }
  g + theme_void() + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(2, 0, 0, 0))
})

# Row weights. A is the trace and needs range because its range IS the data; C spans decades; G is
# points over lag. Head at 0.15, deliberately a little less than the two lines of text need, so the
# empty panel under the titles collapses and they sit flush against row A.
#        head   A     B     C     D     E     F     G
# REDISTRIBUTED 2026-08-12. The canvas is fixed at 5.90 in, so these are shares and not lengths:
# raising the total from 4.85 to 4.90 shrinks every unit by 1% and the whole effect is in who gets
# more of it. A 0.85 -> 0.75, D and E 0.60 -> 0.65, F 0.70 -> 0.75. Measured, at 5.728 in of grid:
#   A 1.004 -> 0.877 in (72 -> 63 pt)      D 0.709 -> 0.760 in (51 -> 55 pt)
#   E 0.709 -> 0.760 in (51 -> 55 pt)      F 0.827 -> 0.877 in (60 -> 63 pt)
#   B, C and G each lose about 1 pt.
# WHY THOSE ROWS. The y-axis labels are rotated, so their LENGTH is measured against the ROW HEIGHT,
# and D, E and F carry the three longest of the seven, the longest being F's Var(Sigma s_t)/Sigma
# F_t. A can afford to pay: it is the tallest row by far and its y range already carries 45% of
# added headroom for the logL annotation (yTr below), which is set as a fraction of the data range
# and so does not move when the row gets shorter. A stays the tallest row, tied with F at 0.877 in.
HS <- c(0.15,  0.75, 0.55, 0.70, 0.65, 0.65, 0.75, 0.70)
ROWS <- list(A = pA, B = pB, C = pC, D = pD, E = pE, F = pF, G = pG)
nc   <- length(STEPS) + 2
# The rotated row-title strip stays, at six columns too (Luciano, 2026-07-31): matching the parent
# figure's furniture is worth more than the width it costs. What it costs is measured, not guessed:
# the strip is 0.47 in, so with it and the second block's y axis the fixed furniture is 1.90 of the
# 7.0 in and the panels land at 0.85 in; dropping it would buy 0.08 in per panel. That is not
# enough to be worth having the supplement look like a different family of figure from its parent.
STRIP <- TRUE
cells <- unlist(lapply(names(ROWS), function(k)
  c(list(rowlet(k)), ROWS[[k]],
    if (STRIP) list(rowstrip(RTTL[[k]], RSTRIP_FILL[[k]],
                             RSTRIP_YMIN[[k]], RSTRIP_YMAX[[k]])))), recursive = FALSE)
grid <- wrap_plots(c(
    list(plot_spacer()), lapply(STEPS, colhead), if (STRIP) list(plot_spacer()), cells),
  ncol = nc,
  # ABSOLUTE widths for the two furniture columns, null for the panels. figure_3 sets them as
  # FRACTIONS of a panel (0.085 and 0.155), which is the same thing only at its own column count:
  # a fraction of a 1.31 in panel is 0.11 and 0.20 in, but a fraction of the 0.85 in panel six
  # columns leave is 0.07 and 0.13, and the rotated two-line row title does not fit in 0.13 -- it
  # rendered clipped. The strips carry TEXT, so what they need is a length, not a proportion.
  widths = unit(c(0.112, rep(1, length(STEPS)), if (STRIP) 0.203),
                c("in", rep("null", length(STEPS)), if (STRIP) "in")),
  heights = HS)
# The key is STACKED UNDER the whole grid, not placed in a cell of it. In a cell its 0-to-1
# coordinates map to one column's 1.78 in and every label overprints its neighbour, which is what
# the first render did.
KEYH <- if (length(PSEL) > 1) 0.030 else 0.018
g <- grid / keyplot + plot_layout(heights = c(1, KEYH))
# HEIGHT 5.90 in, was 7.5 (2026-08-05). At 7.5 the float ran 185 pt past the page and LaTeX dropped
# the last 109 words of the legend and both supplement lines off the bottom. The legend is also being
# cut by about a hundred words in the same pass; the two together close the deficit. Point sizes do
# not scale with the device, so this shortens the panels and leaves the text at its set size.
FIGH <- 5.90
ggsave(OUT, g, width = 7.0, height = FIGH)
# The message used to say 7.5 in, hardcoded, and stayed that way when the height went to 5.90 on
# 2026-08-05. It cost an afternoon in 2026-08-12's caption-fitting pass, where the page budget was
# computed from the message instead of from the artefact. It now prints the variable.
cat(sprintf("wrote %s: 7 rows, %d members, parameters %s, 7.0 x %.2f in\n",
            OUT, length(STEPS), paste(names(PSEL), collapse = " + "), FIGH))
```
